mainEntity.name: How soon after a wildfire smoke event should I have carpet cleaned?

acceptedAnswer.text: Within 60 days for the best extraction results. PM2.5 particles bond more firmly to synthetic carpet fiber over time — especially after cycling through Medford's 90–110°F summer heat. Cleaning within 60 days produces significantly better results than cleaning 3–6 months after the event. If you've had multiple smoke events this season, book after the first major event rather than waiting until fall.

mainEntity.name: Can you clean carpet during an active smoke event?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes — we schedule and clean during active fire seasons. The key variable is ventilation: we clean when AQI allows windows to be opened for the drying window (AQI below 100). For days with AQI above 100, we schedule cleaning for the next clear day. Book during the event to get the earliest post-event appointment slot. Check OregonAQI.com for current conditions.

mainEntity.name: What's the difference between your wildfire protocol and standard cleaning?

acceptedAnswer.text: The wildfire smoke protocol uses an oxidizing pre-spray with a minimum 8-minute dwell time before 195°F truck-mounted extraction. The oxidizing chemistry chemically converts PM2.5 VOC compounds — breaking the molecular bonds between smoke particles and carpet fiber — before extraction removes them. Standard cleaning reduces smoke odor; the wildfire protocol addresses the source. Learn more

mainEntity.name: My carpet smells like smoke even after being cleaned once — what's happening?

acceptedAnswer.text: Several possibilities: the previous cleaning used standard protocol rather than smoke-specific protocol; PM2.5 embedded at fiber depth wasn't fully addressed; or the HVAC ducts are redistributing smoke compounds back into the freshly cleaned carpet every time the system runs. Why carpet smells after cleaning and air duct cleaning

mainEntity.name: Does wildfire smoke affect all carpet types the same way?

acceptedAnswer.text: No — synthetic carpet (nylon, polyester, olefin) bonds PM2.5 compounds through a different chemical mechanism than wool or natural fiber rugs. Synthetic fiber's polymer structure provides more bonding sites for PM2.5 VOC compounds. Natural fiber rugs require a different pre-spray approach — not the oxidizing formula, which can damage wool. We assess fiber type at pre-inspection and adjust protocol accordingly. Wool rug guide
